analysis.one_liner: Gives free insulin cards to uninsured people and taxes insulin makers that spike prices.
analysis.headline: The Emergency Access to Insulin Act was introduced in the Senate in May 2023, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a grant program helping states, tribes, and tribal organizations run "insulin card" programs that let uninsured and underinsured people get insulin at no cost from pharmacies. To pay for it, it would charge insulin manufacturers an annual fee based on their market share, equal to the program's total cost. It would also impose a tiered tax — 50%, 75%, or 100% of the extra revenue — on insulin makers whose prices rise faster than inflation, cut the exclusive market period for new biological drugs from 12 years to 7 to speed up cheaper generic competition, and count program payments toward high-deductible plan deductibles.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured people with diabetes who need insulin — an estimated 8+ million Americans with diagnosed diabetes lack adequate coverage. The bill would let them get a 7-day emergency supply within five business days and a renewable 90-day supply at no cost, with payments counting toward their insurance deductible so they are not stranded mid-deductible. People on any insurance eventually benefit too: the shorter 7-year exclusivity for biological drugs opens the market to cheaper copies years sooner, and the price-spike tax makes large insulin price increases unprofitable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured people who need insulin

how_it_helps.text: Grants to states, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations would fund insulin card programs under which pharmacies fill prescriptions at no cost for uninsured or underinsured individuals, with a 7-day emergency card issued within 5 business days and a renewable 90-day card within 12 business days.

For underinsured people in high-deductible plans, payments made through the program would count toward their deductible or other out-of-pocket requirements, so free insulin does not leave them further behind on their plan.

Insulin manufacturers would pay annual fees (2024-2028) allocated by market share, equal to the total cost of the assistance program, so the program is funded by the companies whose product is being provided.

A tiered excise tax would apply when an insulin price rises faster than inflation: 50% of the price-spike revenue for smaller spikes, 75% for 15-20%, and 100% for spikes of 20% or more, with a cumulative multi-year version that targets chronic price creep, and no exemption for companies that threaten to curtail production.
The exclusivity period for biological drugs would be cut from 12 years to 7 years, allowing cheaper biosimilar competition for new biologics — not just insulin — years earlier.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers would bear the direct costs: annual fees equal to the full program cost, an excise tax of up to 100% of revenue gained from inflation-beating price increases, quarterly price reporting with civil penalties for late filing, and a shortened exclusivity window that invites biosimilar competition years earlier. States and tribes would also have to contribute $1 in non-federal money for every $3 of federal grant funds. Taxpayers would absorb any program costs not covered by the fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insulin manufacturers, plus state matching funds

drawbacks.text: States and tribes must put up $1 in non-federal money for every $3 of federal funds to receive a grant, which could keep financially strapped states — often those with the most uninsured residents — from participating at all.

The program is not permanently funded: appropriations are open-ended rather than guaranteed, and the grant authority sunsets five years after enactment, so the assistance would disappear unless Congress renews it.

The bill exempts prices paid under the insulin card program from Medicaid's 'best price' and average manufacturer price rules, a concession to manufacturers that slightly weakens one of the government's main levers for keeping Medicaid drug costs down.

Because the exclusivity cut from 12 to 7 years applies to all biological drugs, the strongest good-faith objection is that shorter protected market periods could reduce the return on developing new biologic medicines, though it also accelerates cheaper copies of every new biologic.

The price-spike tax targets wholesale price increases above inflation, so manufacturers could legally raise prices slowly, year after year, staying just under the inflation benchmark without triggering any tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and immediate: insulin is a life-sustaining drug that people die without, and the card program directly removes cost as a barrier for the uninsured and underinsured. The costs fall overwhelmingly on a single, highly profitable industry, plus a modest state matching requirement that is the bill's most serious design flaw. The 12-to-7-year exclusivity cut is a structural pro-competition change that trades some theoretical reduction in innovation incentive for faster access to cheaper drugs. On balance this is a well-targeted consumer bill whose main weaknesses are its temporary funding and the state match, not its core design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on May 9, 2023.
That same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over taxation and health programs.
No other senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it, as any bill not passed by both chambers does.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers are better off: they pay no market-share fee, face no price-spike tax, keep the full 12-year exclusivity period for new biologics, and no publicly funded insulin card program competes with their direct sales to uninsured patients.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin manufacturers, who keep pricing power

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Access to Insulin Act of 2023 and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; it received no hearing, no committee vote, and was never sent to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No party-line split was ever recorded: the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill charges insulin makers annual fees covering the entire cost of the assistance program, taxes up to 100% of revenue from inflation-beating price spikes, and subjects them to quarterly price reporting with penalties. Because insulin prices in the U.S. have historically risen far above inflation, these provisions directly cap a major pricing practice that generates revenue at the expense of patients.

Cutting biologic exclusivity from 12 years to 7 years applies to every new biological drug, not just insulin, letting biosimilar competition — and lower prices — arrive up to five years sooner. The industry's interest in longer protected market periods runs against the public's interest in cheaper drugs.
States would enter agreements with pharmacies to fill insulin prescriptions for card holders and pay the pharmacies for the insulin dispensed, creating a new public payer for those fills.
